title: Innate immunity
covers: Where immune cells come from, the cells and receptors of innate immunity, and its three effector mechanisms: phagocytosis, inflammation and NK-cell killing.

items.p: The immune system keeps the organism intact. It protects against pathogens and danger signals, and it takes part in cancer prevention and defense.
Innate immunity is the first line of defense. It acts within hours, before the adaptive response (days) is ready.

ul: Recognizes common patterns, not specific antigens
Rapid: present before exposure or reacts immediately
No clonal expansion and no memory
Not transferable
Stimulates and shapes adaptive immunity

items.p: Most immune cells are made in the bone marrow. T cells are made there too, but mature in the thymus.
Some tissue-resident macrophages, such as microglia in the CNS, come from the yolk sac or fetal liver during embryonic life.

ul: Primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow and thymus
Secondary lymphoid organs (where cells do their work): lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils, mucosal tissue
Myeloid progenitor: megakaryocyte/erythrocyte and granulocyte/macrophage lines, mast cells, dendritic cells
Lymphoid progenitor: T cells, B cells, NK cells
Avoidance: barriers, physical and chemical (antimicrobial proteins)
Resistance: effector mechanisms that attack the pathogen
Tolerance: the tissue becomes better at resisting damage, without lowering pathogen fitness

items.p: Disease tolerance is not the same thing as immunological tolerance.

table: Lives in tissues; main phagocyte there; orchestrates the response with inflammatory mediators
Circulates; short-lived; most numerous innate cell; main phagocyte; dies after entering tissue
Third phagocyte; main job is antigen presentation (best APC) and activating other cells
Parasites too large to ingest; allergic inflammation
Matures in skin, gut and airway mucosa; histamine granules; worms and type I allergy
Innate lymphoid cell (group I); kills tumor and virus-infected cells; early antiviral defense

items.p: Small proteins (about 25 kDa) released after a stimulus. They act through specific receptors.

ul: Autocrine: same cell. Paracrine: neighbors. Endocrine: distant cells through blood.
Families: IL-1, interferons, TNF, hematopoietin
Hematopoietin receptors signal through JAK kinases, which activate STAT transcription factors

items.p: Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) detect PAMPs from pathogens and DAMPs from damaged tissue.

Injured tissue releases metalloproteinases and hyaluronidases. They cut the extracellular matrix, and the fragments trigger inflammation. Necrosis releases many DAMPs; apoptosis releases few and is cleared silently.

ul: TLRs: on the plasma membrane or in endocytic vesicles; sense extracellular microbial products; activate NFκB and IRF, giving inflammatory cytokines and type I interferons
Humans have 10 TLRs. TLR-4 senses LPS of Gram-negative bacteria.
NLRs: cytoplasmic sensors; some activate NFκB, others form an inflammasome (NLRP3) with cell death and pro-inflammatory cytokines

items.note: The slide lists lipoteichoic acid as sensed by TLR-1:TLR-2 and TLR-4. Standard texts give TLR-2 heterodimers for lipoteichoic acid and keep TLR-4 for LPS. Answer the exam from the slide.

items.p: Receptors that trigger uptake: complement, Fc, scavenger and C-type lectin receptors. G-protein coupled receptors drive cytokine production.

ul: Bind, engulf (membrane zips up), phagosome, fusion with lysosome, phagolysosome
Killing: lysosomal enzymes, reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide (iNOS: arginine to citrulline)
NADPH oxidase: O2 to superoxide. Deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease.
Superoxide dismutase: superoxide to H2O2. Myeloperoxidase: H2O2 plus chloride to HOCl.
NADPH comes from G6PD (HMP shunt)

items.p: NK cells kill without priming. The decision is a balance between two kinds of receptor.

ul: Inhibitory receptors recognize MHC I on healthy cells: no killing
Infected or tumor cells often lose MHC I: the brake is gone
Activating receptors recognize stress molecules on infected or tumor cells; a strong signal can override inhibition
Killing: perforin and granzymes from cytotoxic granules
NK cells also secrete IFNγ and TNFα, which boost macrophages and dendritic cells

cards.q: Which lymphoid organs are primary, and which are secondary?
cards.a: Primary: bone marrow and thymus. Secondary: lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils, mucosal lymphoid tissue.

cards.q: Where do microglia come from?
cards.a: Yolk sac or fetal liver, during embryonic development (not from bone marrow monocytes).

cards.q: Five features of innate immunity
cards.a: Pattern recognition, rapid, no clonal expansion, no memory, not transferable (and it shapes adaptive immunity).

cards.q: Avoidance, resistance, tolerance: what does each mean?
cards.a: Avoidance = barriers. Resistance = effector mechanisms against the pathogen. Tolerance = tissue resists damage better, pathogen fitness unchanged.

cards.q: Which cell is the most numerous innate cell and a short-lived main phagocyte?
cards.a: Neutrophil

cards.q: Main role of dendritic cells
cards.a: Antigen presentation (best APC) and mediators that activate other immune cells; not clearance of microbes.

cards.q: Cells for parasites too large to phagocytose
cards.a: Eosinophils and basophils (mast cells protect surfaces against worms)

cards.q: Where do mast cells mature, and what do their granules hold?
cards.a: In peripheral tissues (skin, intestine, airway mucosa); histamine.

cards.q: What makes innate lymphoid cells different from lymphocytes?
cards.a: They lack antigen-specific receptors. NK cells are group I ILCs.

cards.q: Hematopoietin-family cytokine receptors signal through...
cards.a: JAK tyrosine kinases, which activate STAT transcription factors.

cards.q: PRR ligands: two classes
cards.a: PAMPs (pathogen) and DAMPs (damaged host tissue)

cards.q: Which enzymes generate DAMPs from extracellular matrix?
cards.a: Metalloproteinases (MMPs) and hyaluronidases (HYALs)

cards.q: TLRs: location, and transcription factors activated
cards.a: Plasma membrane or endocytic vesicles; NFκB and IRF (inflammatory cytokines, type I interferons)

cards.q: Which TLR senses LPS?
cards.a: TLR-4

cards.q: NLRs: location and the named inflammasome
cards.a: Cytoplasmic; NLRP3 inflammasome (cell death and pro-inflammatory cytokines)

cards.q: NADPH oxidase deficiency causes...
cards.a: Chronic granulomatous disease (no superoxide in the respiratory burst)

cards.q: Which enzyme makes hypochlorous acid in the phagolysosome?
cards.a: Myeloperoxidase (from H2O2 and chloride)

cards.q: How do phagocytes make nitric oxide?
cards.a: iNOS converts arginine to citrulline, releasing NO.

cards.q: What switches an NK cell off?
cards.a: Inhibitory receptors recognizing MHC I on a healthy cell.

cards.q: Why are virus-infected and tumor cells vulnerable to NK cells?
cards.a: They often lose MHC I (no inhibitory signal) and show ligands for activating receptors.

cards.q: How do NK cells kill, and which cytokines do they secrete?
cards.a: Perforin and granzymes; IFNγ and TNFα.

cards.q: NK cells versus cytotoxic T cells: priming
cards.a: NK cells kill without priming; cytotoxic T cells need priming by antigen-presenting cells.

questions.stem: A host limits damage from an infection by increasing a tissue's capacity to resist microbe-induced injury, without reducing the pathogen load. Which host strategy is this, and how does it differ from the other two?

options.E: Tolerance; avoidance relies on barriers and resistance on effector mechanisms

options.D: Perforin and granzymes, acting on macrophages and dendritic cells
options.E: IFNγ and histamine, acting on eosinophils and basophils

questions.explanation: NK cells secrete cytokines such as IFNγ and TNFα, which act on other immune cells like macrophages and dendritic cells. A: The slide names macrophages and dendritic cells. C: The cytokines named are IFNγ and TNFα. D: These are cytotoxic granule contents, not the cytokines. E: Histamine is a mast cell mediator.

questions.stem: What decides whether an NK cell kills a target cell?

options.B: Presentation of peptide on MHC class II
options.C: Prior priming by dendritic cells
options.E: Deposition of complement on the target

questions.explanation: NK decision = balance of activating and inhibitory receptors; activating receptors recognize molecules on cancer and infected cells. A: NK cells lack one. B: Helper T cells. C: Not needed. E: Not the decision.

questions.stem: A healthy hepatocyte with normal MHC I is not attacked by NK cells, whereas a virus-infected hepatocyte that has lost MHC I is lysed. What explains the killing?

options.A: Priming of the NK cell by the virus
options.C: Viral peptide presented on MHC II

questions.explanation: Inhibitory NK receptors recognize cognate MHC I and switch the NK cell off; infected and cancer cells often lose MHC I. A: Not needed. C: Not how NK cells see targets. D: Not needed. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A transformed cell still expresses MHC class I, yet an NK cell kills it. How is this possible?

options.A: Granzymes first cleave its MHC I molecules
options.B: A T cell receptor recognizes it
options.C: Dendritic cells prime the NK cell

questions.explanation: Transformed or infected cells can increase activating ligands, overriding the inhibitory signal even when MHC I is present. A: Not the mechanism. B: NK cells have none. C: Not needed. D: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Within hours of infection, an NK cell lyses a virus-infected cell. What does it release to do this?

options.C: Perforin and granzymes

questions.explanation: NK cells release cytotoxic granules with perforin and granzymes, causing lysis. A: Complement. B: Phagocytes. D: Not NK killing. E: Mast cells.

questions.stem: A child born without a thymus has normal B cells. Where would his T cells normally have matured?

options.C: Lymph nodes

questions.explanation: Most immune cells arise from bone marrow; T cells generated in the marrow mature in the thymus. B: Where T cells are generated, not where they mature. C: Secondary organ. D: Secondary organ. E: Not the site.
